title: Designing for Personal AI Assistants
dek: Seven rules for AI assistants that say less, show more and leave people in control.
readingNote: Every example follows one task: planning dinner with Alex on Thursday at 6:30, at a restaurant called Juniper. The examples are simulations; nothing is recorded, sent or booked.

background.title: Why this guide exists
background.lead: Chatbots and chat boxes have almost ruined everything over the past few years.
paragraphs: Reading endless chat full of filler is exhausting. Even a simple yes-or-no question gets a long explanation, unless you constrain it with a prompt. You read that right: now you get to write the essay.

As models grow more capable, I suspect this isn’t an intelligence problem. It’s a deliberate choice in how agent makers design their products and internal harnesses, and choices can be made differently.
Long conversations and visible reasoning traces may help researchers and trainers find problems. For everyday users, they are a disaster.
Interfaces should take responsibility for presenting information and enabling action, instead of asking people to keep adding prompts and finish the product’s interaction design themselves.
background.takeaway: Use the interaction that fits the moment: voice, real-time voice, generated UI, a briefing. Whatever the moment, the answer should rarely be several long paragraphs.

connections.label: Fit the input to the moment

sections.title: Answer with the smallest thing that works
sections.lead: Match the size of the answer to the size of the question. A yes-or-no question gets a yes or no, plus the one action that follows.
paragraphs: Padding is the most common failure of AI assistants: a friendly preamble, the question restated, a paragraph of caveats, an offer to help further. The answer ends up somewhere in the middle, and the person has to dig for it.
Start with the answer. Add only what changes the person’s decision or next step, and keep everything else a tap or a question away. Nobody should have to write a prompt just to get a shorter reply.

dont.request: Did the invite to Alex go out?
dont.reply: Great question! I’d be happy to give you an update on your invitation. As you requested earlier, I prepared an invitation for dinner with Alex at Juniper on Thursday at 6:30 PM. After you approved it, I sent the invitation to Alex’s email address. Please note that delivery times can vary between email providers, so Alex may not have seen it yet. Is there anything else I can help with, such as setting a reminder?
dont.caption: {count} words to say yes.

do.request: Did the invite to Alex go out?
do.caption: The answer is the first line.

practices.title: Answer first
practices.body: Put the answer, decision or result in the first line. Skip the preamble and don’t restate the question.

practices.title: Budget length by context
practices.body: A glance on a watch, one sentence from a speaker, a short card on a phone. Go longer only when the person asks or the task truly needs it.

practices.title: Keep detail on demand
practices.body: Put reasoning, sources and alternatives behind a clearly labeled control instead of inline.

notice: Both views answer the same question. Compare the word counts.
The card leads with the answer and the action that follows it.
The detail is still there, one tap away rather than in the way.

sections.title: Let the moment choose the input
sections.lead: Voice when hands and eyes are busy, typing when it’s quiet or the words must be exact, a tap when the decision is simple. Switching never starts the task over.
paragraphs: No single input is right everywhere. Speaking is fastest while walking or cooking and awkward on a train. Typing is precise but slow on a watch. Confirming a time is quickest as one tap. Offer the input that suits the situation and keep the others within reach.
Voice needs visible state. When the assistant listens alongside another app, keep that app in front, show whether it is listening, working or done, and make stop a single action.

card.title: I’m listening…
card.body: Your draft is hidden until I finish.

dont.caption: Voice takes over the screen, with no visible way to stop.

do.caption: The draft stays in view. Stop and typing are one tap away.

practices.title: Offer voice, never require it
practices.body: Make voice the fast path where it helps, and keep a visible text field on devices with a keyboard.

practices.title: Switch without starting over
practices.body: Moving between voice, typing and tapping keeps the request and the progress.

practices.title: Show the microphone state
practices.body: Distinguish off, listening, working and speaking, and keep stop and mute one action away.

notice: The email stays in front while the assistant listens.
The control always shows its state: off, listening, working or done.
“Type instead” keeps the words heard so far.

sections.title: Keep one task in front
sections.lead: Give the current task the screen and one next action. Background work reports quietly and waits its turn.
paragraphs: An assistant can run many tasks at once; a person attends to one. Give the task in hand the main view and a single primary action, and keep everything else in a compact activity area.

Background updates shouldn’t steal focus. A price drop or a finished task can wait for a natural pause unless the timing really matters, and nothing should move the button the person is about to press.

dont.caption: Three primary buttons. Which one matters now?

card.title: Does 6:30 work?
card.body: Juniper has a table for two.

do.caption: One decision in front. The price drop waits in the activity row.

practices.title: One primary action
practices.body: Make the step that moves the task forward obvious, with no competing primary buttons.

practices.title: Status, not interruption
practices.body: Show background tasks as small indicators that the person can open when they choose.

practices.title: Interrupt only when it can’t wait
practices.body: Break in only for something that loses value if it waits, such as a table that will be released in five minutes, and say why it couldn’t wait.

notice: The dinner decision owns the view and has one primary button.
Simulate the price drop: it updates the activity row and leaves your focus alone.
Switch tasks with the tabs; each keeps its own state.

sections.title: Recommend one, keep the rest close
sections.lead: Lead with the best answer, give the reason in a line, and keep alternatives one step away. Compare side by side only when comparing is the task.
paragraphs: A long list of options hands the work back to the person. When the assistant knows the preferences, it should commit to a recommendation, explain it briefly and make the next action obvious.
Be specific about uncertainty. A wall of general caveats helps no one. One clear note about what the assistant doesn’t know, and the question that would settle it, does.

dont.request: Where should we have dinner on Thursday?
dont.reply: Here are some great options near you for Thursday evening! 1. Juniper, a modern bistro with a seasonal menu. 2. Olive Room, a lively Mediterranean spot. 3. Little Table, a casual neighborhood café. 4. Harbor Kitchen, seafood with a view. 5. Sakura House, Japanese food that’s good for groups. 6. The Corner Grill, classic comfort food. Each one has its own strengths, so it really depends on your preferences! Let me know which one you’d like.
dont.caption: Six options and no opinion.

do.request: Where should we have dinner on Thursday?

card.title: Juniper
card.body: Quiet, a 12-minute walk, and a table for two at 6:30.
card.note: Not sure: whether Alex eats meat. Juniper has vegetarian dishes.

do.caption: One pick, one reason, one honest unknown.

practices.title: Commit to a recommendation
practices.body: Give the best option a clear position and the action that follows from it.

practices.title: Explain in one line
practices.body: State the reason that matters (quiet, close, free at 6:30) and keep the evidence behind a “Why” control.

practices.title: Name the unknown
practices.body: Flag a specific gap next to the result instead of burying the answer in general caveats.

notice: The recommendation and its action come first.
“Why” and the alternatives open in place, without leaving the result.
The one uncertainty is stated plainly, with a way to resolve it.

sections.title: Show an interface, not a transcript
sections.lead: When a task has structure, such as dates, places or a draft, generate the controls for it inside a familiar frame instead of describing it in another message.
paragraphs: Chat suits open questions. Once a task has a shape, prose becomes a poor interface: reading a paragraph of times to pick an evening, or asking for a rewrite to change one word. Generate a calendar, a comparison or an editor instead.
Keep the frame stable. Navigation, the task name and the assistant input stay where they were while the content changes, and whatever the person selected or typed survives when the view regenerates.

dont.request: When are we both free next week?
dont.reply: You and Alex are both free on the following evenings next week: Monday the 12th after 7:00 PM, Tuesday the 13th between 6:00 and 8:00 PM, Thursday the 15th from 6:30 PM onwards, and Friday the 16th after 8:00 PM. Wednesday the 14th doesn’t work because you have a team dinner. Which of these would you prefer? Just reply with the day and time and I’ll take care of the rest.
dont.caption: A calendar, typed out as prose.

do.request: When are we both free next week?
do.caption: Pick the evening by tapping it.

practices.title: Use the control the data calls for
practices.body: A calendar for dates, a map for places, a table for comparisons, an editor for text.

practices.title: Keep the frame familiar
practices.body: Navigation, task identity and the assistant input stay put while the content adapts.

practices.title: Never lose the person’s edits
practices.body: Regenerating a view keeps selections and typed text, and flags anything that needs a second look.

notice: Schedule, Compare and Edit swap the working view; the frame around them doesn’t move.
Choose another day and an untouched draft updates itself.
Edit the message first, then change the day: your words are kept and flagged for review.

sections.title: Ask before acting, then report what really happened
sections.lead: Show exactly what will change before the assistant acts. While it runs, show real progress. When it stops, say what succeeded, what didn’t and what’s left.
paragraphs: Proposed, in progress, waiting for input, done, failed and partly done are different states, and each needs its own words and controls. Never say “Done” about something that is still running or quietly failed.

Agents increasingly work for minutes, not seconds. Long work needs a visible plan, steps that tick off as they finish, a stop button that keeps working, and a short summary at the end. Not a spinner followed by a wall of text.

dont.request: Book dinner with Alex for Thursday.
dont.reply: All done! 🎉 I’ve taken care of everything for your dinner with Alex on Thursday. Enjoy your evening!
dont.caption: “Done”, but the restaurant hasn’t confirmed.

do.request: Book dinner with Alex for Thursday.

steps.text: Juniper hasn’t confirmed the table yet

do.caption: What’s done, what isn’t, and what to do next.

practices.title: Show the change before approval
practices.body: Name who and what is affected, with the exact values, right next to the approve button.

practices.title: Make long work visible
practices.body: List the steps, update them as they finish, and keep stop available throughout.

practices.title: Report the real result
practices.body: Separate what succeeded, what failed and what still needs the person, with a next action for each.

notice: Before you send, the card shows who, where and when, and nothing has happened yet.
After you send, each step reports its own state, and Stop works until the last one finishes.
The table stays “waiting” until Juniper confirms. Nothing claims success early.

sections.title: Carry the task, not the chat
sections.lead: When someone moves from voice to screen or from phone to laptop, bring the task with them (choices, drafts and progress), not a transcript to scroll back through.
paragraphs: Switching devices shouldn’t mean starting over, or reading back through a conversation to find where things stand. Open the task at the same step, with the same selections and the unfinished draft exactly as it was left.
Be clear about what is kept. Show when a change is still syncing, never overwrite a newer edit with an older one, and keep private details off shared screens.

dont.reply: Welcome back! Here’s everything we discussed about dinner with Alex: 47 messages. Scroll up to pick up where we left off.
dont.caption: The task is in there somewhere.

practices.title: Resume at the same step
practices.body: Restore selections, unfinished input and progress, not the conversation history.

practices.title: Adapt the layout, keep the meaning
practices.body: Use the new device’s space and input while the task stays recognizably the same.

practices.title: Be explicit about sync and privacy
practices.body: Show pending sync, protect newer edits, and keep private content on personal devices.

notice: Change the time or the draft on the phone, then switch to the laptop.
The laptop opens at the same step with the same values. There’s no history to scroll.
The layout changes; the task doesn’t.

devices.title: Across devices
devices.lead: The same task on six kinds of device. Screen size is only one factor: viewing distance, input, shared or personal use and available attention all change how each rule applies.

items.name: Phone
items.context: Personal and in hand, often on the move. Attention comes in short bursts.
rules: A short card: the answer in one line and one button.
Voice and typing are both one tap away; the result stays visible when the keyboard opens.
The current task sits above the assistant input; background tasks fold into a compact activity row.
One recommendation with its action within thumb reach; alternatives a tap away.
Full-width calendars, maps and editors. Let them scroll rather than cramming one screen.
Review the exact change before approving. Dismissing a notification never counts as approval.
Hand off to a laptop at the same step with the same draft; voice-started tasks arrive as editable views.

items.name: Computer & tablet
items.context: Personal and usually seated, with sustained attention and precise input.
rules: More room is not a reason to say more. Keep the answer short and the detail collapsible.
A text field is always visible; voice gets a shortcut and a visible stop.
One active workspace. Other tasks live in a side activity panel, never in competing windows.
Use the space for evidence on demand or a real side-by-side comparison, not a longer list.
Generate richer tools, such as tables, maps and editors, inside the same assistant frame.
Show recipients and values in full before approval. Pressing Enter in a field must never approve.
Open exactly where the phone left off, and flag any edit that is still syncing.

items.name: Watch
items.context: Personal, on the wrist, read in a two-second glance.
rules: A few words and one tap. Anything longer goes to the phone.
Short voice in; a haptic or a single line confirms.
Only the current step. Background results arrive as separate notifications that can wait.
One takeaway. Images, video and comparisons open on the phone.
A compact step, such as picking a time. Never a phone-sized grid.
Approve on the watch only when the full scope fits on the face. Send the rest to the phone.
Show progress and the retained choice. Drafts stay on the phone.

items.name: Smart glasses
items.context: Personal and in the field of view, while the world stays in front.
rules: One line at the edge of view, or one spoken sentence.
Short spoken turns. Switch to the phone to type when speaking is awkward.
One prompt at a time; everything else queues.
Say or show the main takeaway. Visuals open on the phone.
Small task cards only. Maps and editors continue on the phone.
A glance or a casual “okay” is never approval. Ask for a distinct confirmation.
Resume with a short cue that names the task and the retained choice.

items.name: TV
items.context: Shared and across the room. Everyone on the sofa can read it.
rules: Readable from the sofa: one headline and two actions.
Push-to-talk on the remote; type on a paired phone.
One large panel with a clear focus target. Background tasks sit behind an activity entry.
One recommendation. Don’t autoplay generated media while someone is deciding.
Simple panels like a date picker. Dense tables and forms move to a personal device.
It’s a shared screen: keep message text and recipients private, and approve on the phone.
Show a summary that’s safe to share. Private edits continue on the phone.

items.name: Screenless device
items.method: Voice · sound and light cues · physical mute
items.context: Shared or personal, with no screen. Everything is heard.
rules: One sentence, then stop. Offer “more” instead of reading on.
Clear start and stop sounds, and a physical mute that always works.
One spoken thread. Unrelated updates wait for a pause.
Speak one recommendation and name the replies: “Book it, another place, or stop?”
Turn structure into short spoken steps with repeat, back and stop. Send maps and editors to a phone.
Read back the action and values, then require an explicit approval phrase. Silence is not consent.
Recap where things stand in one sentence and offer to continue on a named device.

example.voicePrompt: Book dinner with Alex on Thursday.
example.body: Juniper, Thursday at 6:30, a table for two. Book it, another place, or stop?
